title: Can, want, must
goal: Ask for permission, say what you want and what you have to do, and tackle the two most commonly confused pairs: *vedieť* versus *poznať*, and *nemusieť* versus *nesmieť*.
bekal: use *môcť, chcieť, musieť, vedieť, smieť* followed by the dictionary form
tell *nemusíš* (you don't have to) from *nesmieš* (you mustn't)
ask for things politely with *chcel by som* and *mohli by ste*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Na úrade
dialogs.intro: Budi is renewing his residence permit at the foreign police office. He goes up to an official.

lines.text: Dobrý deň. Chcel by som predĺžiť pobyt.

notes: **Nemusíte doesn't mean "you mustn't".** It means "you don't have to" — it's the obligation that disappears, not the permission. If the official wanted to forbid it, she'd say *nesmiete*. This difference matters at the office, on the street, and in people's homes, and it's explained in full below.

**Chcel by som** is the conditional and the most polite way to ask for anything. It follows the speaker's gender: *chcel by som* (male), *chcela by som* (female). If you learn only one polite phrase from this unit, make it this one.
**Mohli by ste …?** is the most polite way to ask for help — literally "would you be able to …". The shorter *Môžete …?* is also correct and polite enough for most situations.

**Neviem, čo je kolok — but Poznám poštu.** Two verbs for "know" appear side by side in one dialogue. *Vedieť* is for facts and skills; *poznať* is for people, places, and things you've come across. French and German make the same distinction.

**All modal verbs are followed by the dictionary form**, with no linking word: *musím ísť*, *chcem jesť*, *môžem platiť*. There's no equivalent of English *to* in "want *to* eat". Good news — it works like English *must* and *can*: "must go", "can pay".

grammars.title: Five modal verbs
body: All five are irregular, all five are used every day, and all five are followed by the dictionary form. Learn this table whole — it's one of the best investments in all of A1.
after: **Môcť and smieť both mean "may", but they're not the same.** *Môcť* means able **or** allowed — it's broad. *Smieť* specifically means permitted. In everyday speech people use *môcť* for almost everything; *smieť* turns up mainly in official prohibitions and in the negative.

**Vedieť has two jobs**: knowing facts (*Viem, kde býva*) and being able to do something as a skill (*Viem variť*, *Viem po slovensky*). For ability at a particular moment, use *môcť*: *Dnes nemôžem variť* (I can't cook today — no time) is different from *Neviem variť* (I don't know how to cook).
**The past is irregular in two places**: *môcť → mohol/mohla*, *chcieť → chcel/chcela*. The rest are regular: *musel/musela*, *vedel/vedela*, *smel/smela*.

grammars.title: Nemusíš and nesmieš — a difference to learn right now
body: Negating *musieť* and negating *smieť* give two almost opposite meanings. It's one of the few A1 mistakes that can get you into real trouble.

head: Slovak
Meaning
Example
rows: *Nemusíš prísť.* — You don't have to come.
*Nesmieš tu fajčiť.* — You mustn't smoke here.
*Mal by si spať.* — You should sleep.

after: **How to remember it: negating *musieť* cancels the obligation, not the permission.** *Nemusíš prísť* is good news — you're free. *Nesmieš prísť* is a ban — you're forbidden. English has exactly the same trap with *don't have to* and *must not*, so this one should feel familiar.

**Public prohibitions in Slovakia almost always use *nesmie*** or the word *zákaz* (ban): *Zákaz fajčiť*, *Zákaz vstupu* (no entry), *Zákaz parkovania*. If you see the word *zákaz* on a sign, don't do whatever comes after it.
**Nemôžem is used to decline politely**, and it sounds softer than *nechcem* (I don't want to). *Bohužiaľ nemôžem* is the standard way to turn down an invitation without having to explain anything.

head: *vedieť*
*poznať*
rows: a clause or the dictionary form

blocks.text: **Quick check: what comes after it?** If it's followed by a clause (*že…, kde…, čo…, kto…*) or a dictionary form, use *vedieť*. If it's followed by a single noun, use *poznať*. This rule covers nearly every A1 sentence.
**Neviem** on its own is a complete and very useful sentence: "I don't know". *Nepoznám* can also stand alone, but its meaning is narrower — "I don't know that person/thing".

blocks.title: One exception you'll hear a lot
items: *Neviem po slovensky* means "I don't speak Slovak" — a skill, so *vedieť*. But *Nerozumiem* (I don't understand) is used for a particular sentence that was just said.
If someone speaks too fast, the right answer is *Nerozumiem*, not *Neviem*.

blocks.text: The conditional is formed by adding **by** to the past form: *chcel* + *by som* → *chcel by som*. The word *by* sits in second place with the other short words, and it comes before *som/si/sme/ste*: *chcel **by som***, *mohli **by ste***. You don't need the whole system at A1 — the six sentences in this table cover everyday needs.
